title: Education under Yadava Prakashar
body:
Education under Yadava Prakashar

When Swami Ramanujar was very young, he had his upanayanam done. His father, Keshava Dikshitar, attained paramapadam; thus, Swami Ramanujar had to perform his last rites at a very young age. He had not received any formal education and wanted to understand the meaning of the mantras that were being recited. After all the ceremonies were completed, Swami Ramanujar started to receive education from Yadava Prakashar, who was the foremost Advaita guru at the time. Yadava Prakashar's gurukulam was situated in Tiruputkuzhi, which lies outside Kanchipuram. 

Swami Ramanujar used to walk 40 km every day from Sri Perembudur to Kanchipuram to receive an education. One day, in one of the lectures on the Upanishads, the Upanishad Vaakyam stating " Satyam, Jnanam, Anantham Brahma" is said to have been uttered by Yadava Prakashar. It was at this point that one of Swami Ramanujar's classmates asked Yadav Prakashar to give further clarity on the Upanishad Vaakyam. Thus, Yadava Prakashar tells the class that "Satyatvam, Jnanatvam, Ananthatvam are individual characteristics similar to that of the horns of a cow. The horns of a cow can be categorized as Khandatva, Mundatva, and Poornashringatvam. 

According to Advaita philosophy, a man can see that a cow has no horns, half a horn, or has a complete horn. But all three conditions cannot exist at the same time. Similarly, the Lord cannot possess all three qualities at the same time. Thus, the Lord is termed as Nirguna Brahma ."  It is then that Swami Ramanujar poses a question to Yadava Prakashar, saying if I, a student, can sit, can breathe, can listen and question you all at once, why cannot the Lord possess Satyatvam, Jnanatvam, and Anathatvam all at once? Yadava Prakashar was silenced by the question and felt very insulted. Thus, he called off the rest of the lesson for the day. 

The following day, Swami Ramanujar did not attend classes as his mother was not keeping well. The following day, when Swami Ramanujar went to the gurukulam, the students were talking amongst themselves that they had to perform kainkaryam to their Acharya in the form of massaging their Acharya's head. Swami Ramanujar volunteered to apply oil and massage his Acharya's head. As Swami Ramanujar was massaging his Acharya's head, a student asked the Acharya a question. The student asked the Acharya to repeat the previous day's lesson, which was another Upanishad Vaakyam from the Chandogya Upanishad that says " tasya yatha kapyasam pundarikam evam akshini. " This verse describes how the Lord's divine eyes appear. 

Yadava Prakashar begins his explanation by giving an exact translation of the verse by saying His eyes are like those of a monkey's posterior. Swami Ramanujar felt so insulted that he started weeping when he heard this type of comparison being made. Swami Ramanujar then said that this comparison being made is very wrong. 


The word kapyasam in Sanskrit grammar has many meanings. One can be interpreted as the posterior of a monkey. Another interpretation is that of the thin disk of light that envelopes the sun during sunrise. Another interpretation is something that is blown up and out of proportion. When Swami Ramanujar gives these three explanations, he says none of these explanations can be used to describe the eyes of the Lord. Yadava Prakashar gets furious and tells Ramanujar to come to the point and give a so-called befitting explanation that would be better than Adi Shankaracharya's commentary, which says the Lord's eyes look like the posterior of a monkey. 

Swami Ramanujar describes that the word kapi, in Sanskrit, refers to the sun. The word kapyasam refers to kapya: aayasam, which can be described in the following scenario. Imagine a pond with still freshwater, which has lotus flowers blooming in it. When the rays of the sun fall on the surface of the pond, the water evaporates, causing the lotus to bloom with all its resplendence. Thus, the eyes of the Lord can be described as equivalent to those of the sun and possess a gaze that is as soft as the petals of the lotus.
All the students started to praise Swami Ramanujar, and this insulted Yadava Prakashar for the second time. Yadava Prakashar felt so insulted that he decided to kill Swami Ramunjar as he realized that he would become an outstanding personality in the future if nothing were done. 

Thus, Yadava Prakashar planned a field trip to Kashi. On the way somewhere in the vicinity of the Vindya Hills, he told the rest of the students that the next morning, when they would bathe in the river, one student should push Ramanujar's head, and one must push Ramanujar's back so that he would drown. Among the students who were present was Swami Ramanujar's cousin, Govindan. Govindan could not bear to let his cousin die. Thus, in the middle of the night, he woke Ramanujar from his sleep and told him Yadava Prakashar's plans. He then asked him to run away, or he would lose his life. 

Thus, Ramanujar is said to have started running and reached some forests in modern-day Maharashtra. Swami Ramanujar began to look around and realized he was lost beyond any possible help. It was then that he thought that he had to reach Kanchipuram somehow, as he knew the way home from there. 

Then a hunter-huntress couple is said to have come and told Swami Ramanujar that they were coming from Sidhashramam, which is situated in Uttar Pradesh, and said they were traveling towards South India. They decided to travel together in the morning and then sleep. In the morning, when Swami Ramanujar awoke from his sleep, he saw the couple had fled and a group of Vaishnavas, and asked them how he could get to Kanchipuram. 

The Vaishnavas laughed at him and asked him to look ahead, and he would see the gopuram of Varadaraja Perumal Kovil. Swami Ramanujar went to the temple and had darshanam of Sri Varadaraja Perumal and Sri Perundevi Thayaar. When Swami Ramanujar saw Varadaraja Perumal, he saw a close resemblance to the hunter, and when he saw Perundevi Thayaar, he saw a close resemblance to the huntress. Thus, he concluded that the hunter and huntress were none other than Varadaraja Perumal and Perundevi Thayaar, who had come to rescue him from the forest during the night.
